title: Low-Temperature Hybrid Monte Carlo for Perylene and Corannulene: Stabilizing Determinant and Force
authors: Petar Sinilkov, Thomas Luu, Johann Ostmeyer, Finn L. Temmen, Marcel Rodekamp
abstract: We demonstrate a real world physics study of the molecules perylene and corannulene at different doping levels, and calculating selected one-, two- (exciton) and three-body (trion) correlators. This has been done by performing Hubbard-model simulations near room temperature. We find, between charge neutral and doubly charged plateaus of perylene, an interaction-induced $ΔQ = 1$ plateau whose width grows with interaction strength and in which the ground state is a spin doublet rather than a singlet. The algorithmic advancement enabling this study simultaneously stabilizes the determinant and force calculations to machine precision at room temperature, while scaling as well as standard determinant Quantum Monte Carlo simulations of these systems. Furthermore, our formalism retains the full time-displaced (2-point) Green's function, allowing us to construct any $n$-body correlator, including those that contain disconnected diagrams.
summary: This work applies advanced Hybrid Monte Carlo simulations to study the electronic structure of PAHs like perylene using the Hubbard model. The authors report discovering an interaction-driven charge plateau and characterizing the spin state within it. The development of a stable simulation algorithm allows for the calculation of complex multi-body correlation functions at near-zero temperatures.
main_problem: The study investigates the electronic properties and charge transitions in polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) like perylene and corannulene at low temperatures.
main_result: The authors found an interaction-induced $\Delta Q=1$ plateau in perylene, which widens with interaction strength, and determined that the ground state in this plateau is a spin doublet, not a singlet.
method: The research employs Hybrid Monte Carlo (HMC) simulations, which feature an algorithmic advancement stabilizing determinant and force calculations to machine precision.
model_or_system: The system models Perylene and Corannulene using the Hubbard Hamiltonian, incorporating on-site repulsion ($U$) and chemical potential ($\mu$).
key_observables: One-, two- (exciton), and three-body correlators; average charge ($\langle Q angle$) plateaus; average sign ($\langle \Sigma angle$); spin observables ($\langle|S_z|angle$, $\langle S_zangle$).
important_parameters: Interaction strength ($U$), chemical potential ($\mu$), and inverse temperature ($ eta$).
main_assumptions: The method relies on algorithmic advances to stabilize calculations at high inverse temperatures ($ eta$), and the analysis notes potential limitations regarding the sign problem for Corannulene.
figures_summary: Figures demonstrate the sharpening of charge transitions with increasing $ eta$, the widening of the $\Delta Q=1$ plateau with $U$, and the spin state analysis confirming a doublet ground state in the $Q=1$ plateau.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the charge dependence ($\langle Q angle$ vs $\mu$) across different interaction strengths ($U$) and temperatures ($ eta$), calculating various correlation functions to characterize the electronic ground state.
why_interesting: The study provides detailed insights into charge localization and correlation effects in extended $\pi$-electron systems, which are fundamental models for molecular electronics and charge transfer in condensed matter.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Tight-binding lattices of (a) perylene and (b) corannulene, one site per carbon 𝑝𝑧orbital, 𝑁𝑥= 20 each. Filled and open circles are the two sublattices of a two-coloring. It succeeds for perylene, which is bipartite. In corannulene the shaded pentagon and the fifteen-site perimeter are edge-disjoint odd cycles, so at least two bonds (red) must join sites of the same sublattice. Corannulene is shown in projection.

Figure 2: Average charge of perylene against chemical potential, at fixed step size 𝛿= 𝛽/𝑁𝑡≈0.18. (a) Temperature dependence at 𝑈= 2: interacting data (markers) for 𝛽= 10, 30, 50, 70 and 90, with the non-interacting result at each 𝛽(dashed). The smooth ramp of the warm ensembles sharpens into a step function as 𝛽grows. (b) Interaction dependence at 𝛽= 90: the Δ𝑄= 1 plateau appears only for 𝑈> 0 and widens with 𝑈. (c) The corresponding average sign, which stays close to unity for 𝑈= 1 and 2 but collapses for 𝑈= 3.

Figure 3: Spin structure of the 𝑄= 1 region of perylene at 𝑈= 2, 𝛽= 90, 𝑁𝑡= 512. Across the plateau 2 ⟨|𝑆𝑧|⟩rises to unity while 2 ⟨𝑆𝑧⟩stays consistent with zero, identifying the ground state as a spin doublet rather than a singlet. The charge at 𝑈= 2 and 𝑈= 0 is shown for reference.

Figure 4: One-, two- and three-body correlation functions of perylene at 𝑈= 2, 𝛽= 90, 𝑁𝑡= 512: (a) at half filling and (b) in the middle of the 𝑄= 1 plateau, at 𝜇= 0.4688. Panels (c) and (d) mark the chemical potential of each set on the charge curve. At 𝜇= 0 the exciton promotes an electron across the gap; in the plateau it promotes the unpaired electron to the next level. The exciton curve, labelled 𝑆𝑧= 1, is the degenerate triplet partner 𝑐† 𝑘+,↑𝑐𝑙−,↓of (4).

Figure 5: Corannulene at 𝑈= 2, 𝛽= 90, 𝑁𝑡= 512. (a) One-body correlation functions at 𝜇= 0, one color per degenerate pair of levels. For the empty LUMO the added electron propagates cleanly forward in 𝜏; for the filled HOMO and HOMO−1 the forward branch is Pauli-blocked, and the signal is the backward branch, where an electron is removed, plotted against 𝛽−𝜏. The slopes differ because the spectrum of the non-bipartite lattice is not symmetric about half filling. (b) Average charge and (c) average sign against chemical potential: the sign is unity at half filling and collapses exactly where the charge transition happens. Shading marks a severe sign problem, ⟨Σ⟩≤0.2.
